DNA replication. The process by which a cell duplicates its entire genome before cell division. The double helix unwinds, its two strands separate, and each serves as a template for a new complementary strand, producing two identical DNA molecules. Each of these new molecules contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand. This semiconservative mechanism ensures high fidelity, allowing each daughter cell to inherit an exact copy of the parent's genetic code. This mechanism was proven by Meselson and Stahl in nineteen fifty-eight using nitrogen isotopes to track which strands were parental versus newly synthesized. The fidelity is remarkable: mispairing and errors are rare because the template strand enforces correct base pairing.

The machinery is intricate. DNA helicase unwinds the double helix, breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs and creating a replication fork. Primase synthesizes short RNA primers about ten nucleotides long, required because DNA polymerase cannot start synthesis de novo. DNA polymerase then catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation, adding nucleotides in the five prime to three prime direction. DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments and primers to produce a continuous strand. Topoisomerase relieves the tension created by unwinding, preventing the molecule from supercoiling into a knot.

The two strands replicate differently. The leading strand is synthesized continuously in the five prime to three prime direction, the same direction as helicase movement, by a single polymerase. The lagging strand runs three prime to five prime relative to helicase motion, so it is synthesized discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments. In eukaryotes these fragments are one thousand to two thousand nucleotides, each with its own primer. These primers are later removed and gaps filled by polymerase; DNA ligase seals the fragments together.

Replication occurs during the S phase of the cell cycle in eukaryotes. Multiple replication origins, about fifty thousand to one hundred thousand in eukaryotes, ensure the entire genome is replicated in roughly eight hours. Prokaryotes typically have just one origin. Checkpoint controls monitor replication fidelity and completeness; if errors are detected, the cell cycle halts or apoptosis is triggered.

DNA polymerase has three prime to five prime exonuclease activity for proofreading, removing mismatched nucleotides, achieving an error rate of about one per ten billion bases. Mismatch repair systems correct errors that escape proofreading, reducing the overall error rate further to about one per ten billion bases per cell division. Despite this extraordinary fidelity, replication errors accumulate over many divisions, contributing to mutation and evolution. DNA replication is also central to biotechnology: PCR artificially harnesses the replication machinery to amplify DNA exponentially, making replication a cornerstone of molecular diagnostics, forensics, and genetic engineering.
